concept.name: Flattener
concept.definition: A yield curve spread trade that gains when the yield differential between longer-maturity and shorter-maturity rates decreases (the curve flattens or inverts). It is executed short the front (shorter-maturity) leg and long the back (longer-maturity) leg, typically DV01-neutral using Treasury futures or cash bonds.
concept.intuition: You are betting the gap between long-term and short-term rates shrinks — again, independent of whether the overall rate level rises or falls.
concept.mechanics: Sell the spread: short the short-end instrument and long the long-end instrument. As with the steepener, legs are ratioed so the position is DV01-neutral, isolating the change in the yield differential; CME Group lists fixed-ratio curve spreads to remove legging risk and obtain margin offsets.
concept.formula: Curve spread = y_long_maturity - y_short_maturity; flattener P&L approx = -(change in spread in bp) * position DV01.
concept.failure_modes: Flattening can stall for long periods, leaving the position exposed to negative carry and roll on the futures legs. DV01 neutrality does not protect against non-parallel kinks (e.g. the 5-year point moving independently) or against convexity differences between the two legs.
concept.misconceptions: A flattener does not require the curve to fully invert to profit — any narrowing of the spread helps. It is also not equivalent to simply shorting bonds: a parallel rise in yields is designed to wash out, leaving only the relative move.
concept.example: Ahead of expected Fed hikes, a trader shorts 2-year futures and buys 10-year futures DV01-neutral; as front-end yields rise faster than long-end yields and 2s10s narrows from 80 bp to 30 bp, the position gains roughly 50 bp times DV01.

citations.source: CME Group: Yield Curve Spread Trades - Opportunities & Applications
